Discuss how the value of the denominator impacts the final value, highlighting how the value is smaller as the denominator increases.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Fractions decimals and percentages_12_Convert fractions, decimals and percentages
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on prior knowledge to confidently convert between fractions, decimals and percentages. Encourage students to use a combination of calculator and non-calculator methods. Remind them that fractions represent division and that percentages are out of 100, which can support conversions to fractions or decimals. A recap of place value may also be useful when converting decimals to fractions, for example recognising that 0.12 represents 12 hundredths or 12 100

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Fractions decimals and percentages_1_Represent tenths and hundredths
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students recognise tenths and hundredths when represented with a diagram. Students explore diagrams such as number lines to see how tenths represent a whole divided into ten equal parts. They also look at how many hundredths are equivalent to one tenth. By introducing a hundred square as having an overall value of 1, students can determine that one small square is equivalent to 0.01 and 1 100 and hence make equivalent connections between hundredths and tenths. It is important that students can complete a visual representation as well as write in numerals and words what a given diagram represents.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Fractions decimals and percentages_2_Number lines with fractions and decimals
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of using both fractional and decimal number lines and transition smoothly between the two. Start with number lines that range from 0 to 1 with ten equal increments, before progressing to number lines with different start and end values. Students also explore double number lines with both fraction and decimal values. Remind them about equivalences established from the previous step, for example 7 10 = 0.7 and model how both can be represented on a number line.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Fractions decimals and percentages_3_Tenths, hundredths, fifths and quarters
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students reinforce their understanding of tenths and hundredths, while also exploring fifths and quarters. Draw attention to equivalences such as 10 100 = 1 10 = 0.1 and 2 10 = 1 5 = 0.2. Highlight the link between tenths and fifths, which can then be used to convert other values such as 3 5 to decimals. Students then progress to working with quarters, using 25 100 = 1 4 = 0.25 to convert other values such as 3 4 Representations such as hundred squares and number lines are useful to build conceptual understanding.

In this small step, students deepen their understanding of percentages by exploring the relationship between fractions and percentages. Emphasise that “per cent” means “per hundred”. For example, 27% represents 27 out of 100. Use a hundred square to illustrate this visually. Students practise writing the percentage of shaded and unshaded regions, recognising that 100% represents a whole. Encourage them to first express amounts as fractions, such as 27 100, before converting to percentages. Students then progress to interpreting diagrams divided into other equal parts, such as 20

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Fractions decimals and percentages_6_Convert simple fractions, decimals and percentages
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students draw together their knowledge from the previous steps in this block and gain fluency in converting between simple fractions, decimals and percentages. The focus remains on familiarity with commonly seen fractions, decimals and percentages, rather than rote memorisation of a technique for any value. In particular, students should be confident in converting multiples of 10% and 25% given in any form. Start with identifying the fraction, decimal and percentage of shaded parts in diagrams, such as hundred squares and bar models, before progressing to more abstract conversions.

In this small step, students identify non-linear relationships in graphs where the data points do not follow a straight-line pattern, but instead show a non-linear relationship between the variables. Students should focus on determining whether there is a relationship between the variables, even if it is not linear. A non-linear relationship may show a curve or other patterns that still indicate a correlation. For example, a U-shaped graph demonstrates that while a line of best fit cannot be drawn, there is still a clear relationship between the variables. It is important to recognise that a non-linear correlation does not mean that there is no relationship at all, as the data points may still follow a consistent pattern. Understanding non-linear relationships helps students to differentiate between different types of correlation and to interpret data more accurately.

In this small step, students construct and interpret composite bar charts. Establish that in a composite bar chart, each bar represents a total, and each section of the bar a sub-category. Start with a composite bar chart with two sub-categories, for example the sales of orange juice and apple juice over a weekend. Orange juice and apple juice are the sub-categories, and the complete bar represents the total sales of drinks each day. Ensure that students understand how to compare sub-categories across the bars and can determine the frequency of sub-categories. Give students opportunities to discuss the differences between composite, dual and standard bar charts.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Graphing data_5_Coordinates in the first quadrant
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students read and plot coordinates in the first quadrant, building on their knowledge of coordinates from Key Stage 2 Recap key terms relating to a coordinate grid, such as the origin, the x-axis and the y-axis. Establish that a coordinate grid is used to describe and accurately show the position of points. Demonstrate how to read coordinates by first moving horizontally along the x-axis and then vertically along the y-axis. Emphasise that coordinates are written as (x, y), with the x-coordinate always coming first. Once students are confident in reading coordinates, they can plot points on the grid and explore coordinate grids with different scales on the axes.

In this small step, students draw scatter graphs and interpret relationships between data sets. Explain that scatter graphs display how two sets of data relate, using pairs of coordinates plotted on a graph. Everyday examples, such as height versus shoe size, can help to make this more relatable. Explain the role of each axis in context and emphasise that every point represents a specific pair of values. Initially, provide pre-drawn axes to support students and then discuss how to select an appropriate scale for each axis, encouraging them to draw their own. Guide students to identify patterns in the data and to describe the relationships. Explore scatter graphs with positive and negative correlation, although correlation is covered in detail in the next step.

In this small step, students examine scatter graphs to determine if there is a relationship between two variables. The relationship is called correlation. Data points with an upward trend show “positive correlation” and a downward trend shows “negative correlation”. If there is no clear pattern, it indicates “no correlation”. Discuss not only the direction of correlation, but also its strength, explaining that strong correlation shows points closely clustered around a trend line, whereas weak correlation shows points more spread out. Use everyday examples, for example temperature versus ice cream sales (positive correlation) or time spent practising versus mistakes made (negative correlation), to make the concept relatable.

In this small step, students draw and interpret lines of best fit on a scatter graph. In Maths, a line of best fit is a straight line that best represents the overall trend between two variables and is used to predict future or missing values. A positive correlation produces a straight upward-sloping line, and a negative correlation a downward slope. If there is no clear correlation, a line of best fit cannot be drawn. Discuss how closely data points cluster around the line to indicate the strength of the relationship. Draw attention to data points that do not follow the general trend. Explain that these are called outliers and discuss possible reasons for these values. It is worth noting that outliers in a scientific context are referred to as anomalous results or an anomaly.

In this small step, students draw and interpret time series graphs. A time series graph is a specific type of line graph used to display data points over time, highlighting trends and changes in a variable. Students should focus on identifying any upward or downward trends, along with periods of stability. Emphasise that while time series graphs highlight overall trends, short-term fluctuations may not always reflect the longer-term trend. Time series graphs with points joined by solid lines imply that it is possible to estimate information between data points, while points joined by dashed lines imply that data between points is not reliable. Discuss different scenarios: for example, estimating the temperature between two recorded points may make sense, but reading values between two years may not always be accurate or useful.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Perimeter and area_1_Convert metric units of length
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on Key Stage 2 learning on converting metric units of length and distance, preparing them for solving problems later in the block. Start by checking that students can identify which metric units are used to measure lengths and choose the most appropriate unit for measuring an item. Draw attention to the size of the metric units, as this will help them to decide when to multiply or divide to complete each conversion. Highlight how the prefix to each measurement can be an indicator of the scale of conversion. For example, “milli-” means “thousandth”, “centi-” means “hundredth” and “kilo-” means “thousand”. If appropriate, challenge students to convert smaller units such as millimetres to micrometres and nanometres.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Perimeter and area_2_Perimeter of a polygon
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the perimeters of 2-D shapes, consolidating and deepening understanding from Key Stage 2 Start with simple, familiar shapes, such as rectangles and triangles. Then progress to irregular polygons such as pentagons and hexagons. Discuss the properties of 2-D shapes in order to promote efficiency. As students’ confidence develops, introduce simple geometric notation such as hatch marks to denote sides of equal length. Challenge students to find unknown lengths given the total perimeter. Encourage the use of calculators, if required, to help focus the learning on calculating the perimeter.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Perimeter and area_3_Perimeter of a compound shape
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the perimeters of compound shapes made up of polygons. Start with compound shapes with all the side lengths labelled, allowing students to build on their prior knowledge of perimeter, before introducing examples with unknown side lengths. Students may split the shapes into their component parts, but the focus should largely be on finding unknown sides using the opposite side lengths. Use simple, recognisable shapes such as rectangles and triangles within the compound shapes. Encourage students to label the diagrams and to write out their calculations clearly.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Perimeter and area_4_Area of rectangles and parallelograms
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students work out the areas of rectangles and parallelograms, building on learning from Key Stage 2 Support students to see the link between shapes, exploring how the parts of a parallelogram can be rearranged to make a rectangle in which the length and width correspond to the base and perpendicular height of the parallelogram. Emphasise that the base can be any of the parallel sides, but the height must be the perpendicular distance between that base and the opposite side. If appropriate, encourage the use of calculators so that the focus remains on finding areas, rather than on the arithmetic. Challenge students to solve problems involving algebraic lengths.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Perimeter and area_5_Area of a triangle
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students work out the area of a triangle using the formula A = 1 2 bh or A = bh 2 , building on learning from Key Stage 2 If necessary, use shapes on a centimetre-squared grid to demonstrate that a triangle is half a rectangle. Students may need support to identify the perpendicular height, particularly when the base is not a horizontal length. Provide standard and non-standard examples in different orientations, so that students become proficient in using the formula and identifying the correct lengths. Challenge them to calculate the length of a base or the perpendicular height given the area of the triangle. Calculators can be used if necessary to help students to focus on using the formula.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Perimeter and area_6_Area of a trapezium
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate areas of trapezia. Ensure that students recognise the properties of a trapezium, using both standard and non-standard examples. Explore the formula for the area by combining two congruent trapezia to form a parallelogram. Use algebraic side lengths to derive the formula A = 1 2 (a + b)h. Encourage students to use the formula whenever possible, rather than splitting the shapes into rectangles and triangles, to promote efficiency. The use of calculators should be encouraged, so that students can become familiar with the formula. If appropriate, they could find an unknown side length from a given area.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Perimeter and area_7_Solve problems with perimeter and area
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students apply their learning from this block to solve problems with area and perimeter. Model the thought processes involved when approaching problem-solving questions. For example, verbalise each step to help students understand how to break down a problem, identify key information and decide which mathematical strategy to apply. Encourage them to clearly label diagrams and to set out their calculations systematically. Examples should be chosen from familiar contexts to ensure understanding and engagement.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Spring__Perimeter and area_8_Form expressions with perimeter and area  E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students use their understanding of area and perimeter to form algebraic expressions. Recap algebraic notation, for example understanding that a × b is written as ab and a × a as a squared, and review how to simplifyexpressions. Start with the areas and perimeters of simple shapes, reinforcing the importance of correctly applying formulae. Initially, use examples involving a single variable before progressing to problems with multiple variables and constants. Encourage students to clearly label diagrams and set out their calculations systematically, to improve accuracyand understanding.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Add and subtract fractions_10_Substitution and solving equations with fractions (E)
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students apply their knowledge of adding and subtracting algebraic fractions within algebraic contexts, including substitution and solving equations. Start by focusing on substituting values into a range of algebraic fractional expressions. It may be helpful to revisit substitution in expressions without fractions before extending to those that include them. Similarly, when solving equations, recap methods for one- and two-step equations before introducing fractional terms, to support understanding. Where appropriate, provide additional challenge by including fractions greater than 1 in substitution problems or equations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may apply the incorrect inverse operation when solving equations. • Students may make errors when substituting into expressions with powers, for example treating p2 as “double p” instead of squaring the value of p. Explain your answer. • What is the inverse of ? • What is a possible first step to solving the equation? • What calculation is equivalent to x2? • Can you collect any like terms before beginning to solve the equation? Explain your answer. • Can the value of an unknown be both negative and fractional? Explain your answer. E

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Add and subtract fractions_1_Simplify a fraction
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of simplifying fractions from Key Stage 2 Students apply understanding of common factors to simplify fractions and recognise when a fraction is already in its simplest form. It may be necessary to revisit factors explicitly to support students who find this step challenging. Emphasise that a fraction is fully simplified when the numerator and denominator share no common factors. Encourage students to simplify in a single step, but also model how fractions can be simplified in multiple steps. Highlight useful strategies, such as noticing when both the numerator and denominator are even, to provide accessible starting points for simplification, before moving on to higher common factors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not notice a common factor when the numerator and denominator are not even. • Students may only partially simplify a fraction. • Students may cancel digits rather than factors, for example simplifying 24 32 to 4 3 by “crossing out 2s”. Year 7 | Summer term | Block 3 – Add and subtract fractions | Step 1 National Curriculum links • Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors (or divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor, lowest common multiple, prime factorisation, including using product notation and the unique factorisation property Mathematical talk • Is the fraction fully simplified? Explain how you know. • What is a common factor of the numerator and the denominator? • Are the numerator and denominator even? How does this help you to decide a potential first step? • Can a fraction be simplified if it contains a prime number? Explain how you know. • How do you simplify the fraction in more than one step? Can you simplify the fraction in one step? • Can a simplified fraction contain a decimal? Explain your answer. • Which is the highest common factor of and ?

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Add and subtract fractions_2_Convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions. Ensure that students understand the difference between a mixed number and an improper fraction. Remind them that a mixed number shows the whole number and a separate fractional part, while an improper fraction expresses the same quantity as a single fraction based on the denominator, with both forms representing values greater than 1. Visual models, such as bar models and number lines, are effective tools for demonstrating the conversion process, as they highlight the total number of wholes alongside the remaining fractional part. Where appropriate, challenge students to generalise a method for conversion, for example a b c = ac + b c . Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that a fraction cannot be greater than 1, as fractions represent part of a whole. • When converting a mixed number to an improper fraction, students may multiply the whole by the numerator and add the denominator, for example 2 2 5 = 9 5 Year 7 | Summer term | Block 3 – Add and subtract fractions | Step 2 National Curriculum links • Use the four operations, including formal written methods, applied to integers, decimals, proper and improper fractions, and mixed numbers, all both positive and negative Mathematical talk • What is a mixed number? • What is an improper fraction? • How can a mixed number be expressed as an improper fraction? • Can you draw a bar model to represent the information? Explain your model. • How many wholes are there in 15 4 ? Explain how you know. What is the remaining fraction? How do you write 15 4 as a mixed number? • How many thirds are there in 2 wholes? Explain how you know. • Is 12 8 greater than 1? Explain how you know. • Is there an equivalent mixed number for every improper fraction? Explain your answer.

small_step_id: Year 7_11-12_Summer__Add and subtract fractions_3_Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, revisiting learning from Key Stage 2 Start by reinforcing the fundamental idea that a fraction represents equal parts, with the denominator indicating how many equal parts the whole is divided into. Bar models provide an effective visual representation, as they can be used to show the total number of equal parts when adding fractions, or the remaining parts when subtracting. Using bar models alongside abstract calculations helps to strengthen students’ conceptual understanding. Students should also work with non-unit fractions and mixed numbers.
