In this extend step, students factorise quadratic expressions, focusing on expressions of the form x2 + bx + c. It can be useful to begin by asking students to find two numbers that make a specific sum and product, for example two numbers that have a sum of 5 and a product of 6 Support students to make connections by explicitly showing that factorising is the inverse of expanding brackets. Initially, focus on positive terms while the concept is developed, before introducing negative terms. Students should understand that a quadratic expression has a maximum of two binomial factors. Using algebra tiles and multiplication grids can strengthen students’ conceptual understanding.

In this small step, students form algebraic expressions, building on the notation and techniques met in Year 7 Students may need reminding that × and ÷ signs are not used in expressions, numbers precede letters and repeated multiplication of a variable is written using exponents (for example, aa is written as a2). Begin by exploring simple expressions such as “5 less than k”, explaining how this differs from “k less than 5”. As students’ confidence develops, move on to writing more complex expressions and apply these to a variety of contexts, such as the perimeter of shapes. To reinforce these concepts, students can use a variety of representations to support understanding, for example concrete resources, such as cubes and counters, and function machines.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Algebraic manipulation_2_Identify and use formulae, expressions, identities and equations
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students cement their understanding of expressions, equations, formulae and identities, before using them in context. Students were introduced to expressions and equations in Year 7 and will have experience of working with formulae in previous blocks such as area, but this is the first time that they explicitly compare and distinguish them. It is important that students know that an identity is true for any value of the variable(s) and includes the symbol æ, whereas an equation is equal only for specific values. A formula differs from an equation as it can be used to find the value of a specific variable, given the value of other variables within the formula. It is worth noting that a formula can be used to generate an equation that can then be solved.

In this small step, students simplify expressions using addition, subtraction, multiplication and division. This step provides an opportunity to build on previous learning of writing algebraic expressions from function machines and collecting like terms. Ensure students are confident with, for example, 5 × b being equivalent to 5b, b ÷ 5 being equivalent to b 5 and b × b being equivalent to b2. This is the extent of any indices work covered in this block, as indices are covered later in the year. Students also need to be familiar with coefficients and understand how they are affected when adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing. It may be helpful to recap the meaning of “like” and “unlike” terms. Encourage students to use the æ symbol.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Algebraic manipulation_4_Use directed number with algebra
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students focus on simplifying expressions and solving equations involving directed numbers. By the end of the step, students should be confident in performing calculations with directed numbers and applying this knowledge to algebraic contexts. Revisiting the use of directed number and solving 1-step and 2-step equations, concepts covered in Year 7, prepares students for more complex expressions later. Double-sided counters are useful tools to support understanding of the four operations with directed numbers. Students may use a calculator, if appropriate.

In this small step, students substitute negative numbers into expressions, building on their prior understanding of substitution and directed number from Year 7 Students need to be confident in recognising the correct order of operations in an expression. Double-sided counters can be a useful representation to aid their understanding. This step aims to develop students’ fluency in using directed numbers, but calculators can be used if the arithmetic is a barrier. Students may need support with entering negative numbers on a calculator and use of the power key.

In this small step, students expand or “multiply out” a single bracket. Students need to know that an expression such as 5(x + 4) means 5 × (x + 4) and that they need to multiply all the terms in the bracket by the coefficient. As students’ understanding develops, introduce negative numbers and variables with coefficients, both inside and outside the brackets. There are many useful ways to represent the expansion of brackets, including bar models, area models and algebra tiles. Each of these can help link multiplication to repeated addition and illustrate the equivalence of expressions.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Algebraic manipulation_7_Factorise into a single bracket
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students factorise expressions into single brackets. Students do not always link factorising expressions with factors of numbers, so it is important to make this connection explicit, reinforcing the vocabulary "common factor" and "highest common factor". It can be useful to practise finding the highest common factor of a variety of terms, including those where a variable is a factor. Show students that factorising is the inverse of expanding a bracket. Begin with examples with positive numerical factors, before progressing to negative factors, algebraic factors and a combination of numerical and algebraic factors. Algebra tiles or area models are useful representations to support students and help them to make connections to their previous work on expanding brackets. Encourage students to check their answers by expanding.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Algebraic manipulation_8_Expand single brackets and simplify
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students simplify expressions with single brackets, building on learning from earlier in the block, applying understanding of expanding brackets, simplifying expressions and zero pairs. Start with expanding and simplifying expressions with a bracket and one other isolated term, for example 3 ± 4(x ± 5). Then move on to expressions with two brackets, for example 3(x ± 4) ± 4(x ± 5). Using concrete resources such as algebra tiles or cubes and counters to represent the expressions can help students to develop an understanding of the difference between similar- looking expressions. Asking them to write an expression to represent the area of a compound shape is an excellent way to apply this skill in context.

Expand double brackets, sometimes referred to as expanding a pair of binomials. Begin with expressions that have all positive terms, before introducing negative terms. Students can also explore expressions in unfamiliar forms such as (x + 2)2 or (x + 2)(3 + x). Discuss the word “quadratic” to help students make links to quadratic graphs and the next step in this block.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_10_Lines of the form y = mx + c
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students further develop their understanding of equations of straight lines of the form y = mx + c. This step focuses on generating coordinates from a table of values and drawing the lines. Reading “y = 3x + 1” as “y is equal to 3 times x plus 1” supports understanding of why, at every point on this line, the y-value is 1 more than 3 times the x-value. Encourage students to explain how their graph is linked to the equation, for example highlighting if the gradient is positive or negative, using what they have covered in previous steps. In this step, students are not required to interpret the gradient and y-intercept from the equation, as this will be covered in Year 9

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_11_Find the midpoint of a line segment E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students build on their knowledge of coordinates to find the midpoint of a line segment. It is useful to first consider the most efficient method of finding the midpoint on a number line before transferring this to working in two dimensions. Students can then explore midpoints of line segments parallel to axes where the start and end points are within the first quadrant. This can be extended to line segments that are not parallel to axes but still in the first quadrant, and then to lines with start and/or end points in other quadrants. Finally, students can explore finding the start or end point of a line segment given the midpoint.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_12_Solve problems with coordinates and graphs E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students apply their knowledge of coordinates, midpoints and graphs of the form y = mx + c to solve a variety of problems. Students may be required to draw on learning from previous blocks to solve problems, for example areas of triangles, properties of 2-D shapes and symmetry. Encourage students to make connections and develop reasoned answers to problems. Modelling the thought process when approaching a problem can be useful in helping students to develop metacognitive skills, enabling them to reflect on and apply similar strategies for themselves. Use goal-free problems to encourage students to develop confidence in problem-solving.

In this extend step, students are introduced to plotting and identifying quadratic graphs. Students initially complete tables of values for quadratic functions, before obtaining coordinates and plotting graphs. Model how to draw a smooth curve to join the coordinates, discussing why it is inappropriate to join the coordinates with straight lines. Initially, focus on graphs with equations of the form y = ax2 and y = x2 ± b, then progress to the form y = ax2 ± b. It is not necessary in this step to draw attention to the effects of the values of a or b on the shape or position of graphs. Quadratic graphs will be explored again in Year 9

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_1_Coordinates in all four quadrants
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore coordinates in all four quadrants, building on the concepts introduced in Year 7 Students further develop their understanding of the x-axis, y-axis and the origin. They may need reminding that the x-coordinate specifies a point’s horizontal position, while the y-coordinate indicates its vertical position. It is important to emphasise the correct naming of the x- and y-coordinates within a coordinate pair, as this is key for recognising equations of lines parallel to the axes. Initially, provide students with pre-drawn axes before they draw their own axes. Encourage them to label each of the four quadrants to help strengthen their understanding.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_2_Lines parallel to the axes
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students are introduced to the idea of a straight line parallel to the axes as an infinite set of points with either a common x-coordinate or a common y-coordinate. Remind students of the term “parallel”. Ensure that they understand that lines parallel to the x-axis have equations of the form y = a and lines parallel to the y-axis have equations of the form x = a. As confidence develops, students can identify which points from a set of coordinates lie on a particular line. Encourage the use of correct mathematical language. For example, reading “y = 3” as “y is equal to 3” helps students to understand why at every point on this line, the y-value is equal to 3. Draw attention to the specific cases x = 0 and y = 0

Complete tables of values for equations of lines. This will prepare them for plotting graphs in forthcoming steps. Before tables of values are introduced, students may need to be reminded of the process of substitution. Start with positive values of x before introducing negative values of x. Ensure that students are confident with the order of operations for equations such as y = 3 + 2x. Students may complete tables of values by spotting patterns, but encourage them to consider the relationship between the x- and y-values from the equation. Links to sequences can be introduced if appropriate.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_4_Recognise and use the line y = x
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students expand their understanding of linear equations by exploring the line y = x, the first diagonal line that they formally study. Prior to this, they have primarily worked with lines parallel to the axes. Students explore why the equation of the line y = x forms a diagonal line, gaining an understanding that this line represents all the points where the x- and y-coordinates are equal. Through this, they identify specific points that lie on the line. Students also compare the lines y = x and y = −x, noting the similarities and differences. Emphasise that these lines form a 45° angle with the axes only when the scales on both axes are the same.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_5_Lines of the form y = mx
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of the line y = x by introducing m and highlighting its effect on the steepness of a line. Students should understand that lines with the equation y = mx form a family of straight lines that all pass through the origin. Reading, for example, y = 5x as “y is equal to 5 multiplied by x” helps students to understand why at every point on the line, the y-value is 5 times the x-value. Use graphical software to explore how increasing or decreasing the value of m affects the graph. Students are not expected to use the word “gradient” to describe the equations of lines yet, as this will be covered later in the block.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_6_Link y = mx to direct proportion E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students build on conversion graphs from the previous block, linking them to equations of lines of the form y = mx. Ensure that students understand the significance of lines passing through the origin in direct proportion relationships. Remind them that conversion graphs can be drawn from tables of values in the same way as lines of the form y = mx. Familiar contexts, such as conversions between litres and millilitres, can be used to introduce the idea of a constant multiplier and hence direct proportion.

In this small step, students build on their understanding of lines of the form y = mx to explore the gradient of a line. Begin by introducing students to gradients of line segments on grids without axes, using the terms “units across”’ and “units up”, before linking to x- and y-directions and the equations of lines. They can calculate the gradient of a straight line by dividing the vertical distance by the horizontal distance between two points on the line. Drawing a right-angled triangle between the two points is a useful strategy. Highlight that they can use any two points on a straight line. Encourage students to write gradients as a fraction when they are not an integer. They can then progress to identifying the gradient given the equation of a line, for example y = 3x has a gradient of 3

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_8_Lines with a negative gradient
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their knowledge of positive gradients and now consider negative gradients. Students extend their understanding of calculating the positive gradient of a line, using a right-angled triangle between two points, and apply this method to lines with negative gradients. Encourage students to recognise the differences and similarities between lines with negative gradients and those with positive gradients. When exploring lines drawn on axes, use the language of “y-values decreasing as x-values increase” and contrast with increasing y-values for positive gradients.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Coordinates and graphs_9_Lines of the form y = x + c
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consider the impact of adding or subtracting a constant to or from the line y = x. Students initially use a table of values to form a set of coordinates and then plot the graph. Encourage them to compare lines and to explore the effect of the value of c on the position of the line. The use of graphical software can support students to recognise the effect of these changes and encourage discussion. Students should be able to look at an equation of the form y = x + c and identify the y-intercept, as well as write the equation given the y-intercept. Draw attention to the fact that all the lines of the form y = x + c are parallel.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Multiply and divide fractions_1_Multiply a fraction by an integer
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students multiply a fraction by an integer. Begin by making links between repeated addition and multiplication to support understanding of why only the numerator is multiplied by the integer. Representations such as bar models or number lines can be used to support. Initially, explore multiplying unit fractions by an integer and remind students that multiplication is commutative, for example 5 × 1 7 = 1 7 × 5. As students’ confidence develops, progress to multiplying non-unit fractions. If necessary, recap simplifying fractions and converting between improper fractions and mixed numbers before exploring multiplications that involve these skills.

In this small step, students build on learning from the previous step, focusing on multiplying a fraction by a fraction. Folding paper or using an area grid as a representation can help students to understand why multiplying a fraction by a number less than 1 results in a smaller product. Encourage them to make connections between the numerators and denominators in the calculation and answer. As their confidence develops, students can work with calculations that require simplification. If appropriate, they could look for common factors in the numerator of one fraction and the denominator of the other fraction and simplify them before multiplying.

In this small step, students learn how to find and use the reciprocals of fractions, integers and decimals. Start with multiplying unit fractions and integers, for example one third × 3 and 4 × one quarter, asking students what they notice about the product of the unit fraction and the integer. Ask them to find other integers and unit fractions that multiply to make 1, before exploring cases with non-unit fractions. Establish that any two numbers that have a product of 1 must be reciprocals of each other. Lead students to spot that reciprocals of proper and improper fractions are easily identified by inverting the numerator and denominator. They may need a reminder of how to express mixed numbers and decimals as fractions before finding reciprocals of these.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Multiply and divide fractions_5_Divide a fraction by an integer
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students divide a fraction by an integer, building on learning from Key Stage 2 Use bar models to support students’ visualisation of the calculation processes. Start with simple examples where the numerator is a multiple of the integer, for example 6 7 ÷ 2. As understanding develops, progress to examples where the numerator is not a multiple, for example 5 8 ÷ 3. It can be helpful to demonstrate how both the equivalent fractions method and the reciprocal method achieve the same result. Discuss how the reciprocal method becomes particularly useful in more complex problems and explain that it provides a more general approach to fraction division.

In this small step, students learn to divide a proper fraction by a proper fraction, consolidating the methods taught in previous steps. It may be helpful to recap multiplying fractions and finding the reciprocal of a number. Students have learned to divide fractions by converting them to have the same denominators and then dividing the numerators, as well as rewriting the division as a multiplication by the reciprocal of the divisor. In this step, they should focus on identifying the most efficient method for dividing fractions rather than relying on mnemonics such as “KFC” (keep, flip, change). While such shortcuts may provide a quick fix, they do not help students to develop a deeper understanding of the process. Instead, they should think about when to apply the reciprocal method and how it relates to the concept of division.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Multiply and divide fractions_8_Multiply and divide mixed numbers
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of using proper fractions to multiply and divide mixed numbers. Ensure that students can confidently convert between mixed numbers and improper fractions before attempting to multiply and divide them. Start by multiplying a mixed number by an integer, supporting students by linking multiplication with repeated addition. As their confidence grows, explore multiplying and then dividing mixed numbers. Bar models or circles can illustrate division using the grouping definition, for example how many 2 3 go into 2 2 3 . Remind students that finding the reciprocal of a mixed number is easier when it is written as an improper fraction. If appropriate, students could explore cross-simplifying fractions before multiplying to simplify calculations.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Multiply and divide fractions_9_Multiply and divide algebraic fractions E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: Multiplying and dividing fractions with algebraic fractions. Students may need reminding of algebraic notation, for example a × c æ ac and 2x × x æ 2x2. Begin by comparing the product of a numerical fraction and an integer, and of an algebraic fraction and an integer, for example two thirds × 4 = eight thirds and x 3 × 4 æ 4x 3 . Then move on to the product of two fractions, for example two thirds × four fifths = 2 × four thirds × 5 = eight fifteenths and a b × c d æ a × c b × d æ ac bd . As students’ confidence develops, introduce calculations that require simplifying, such as 2x 3 × 3y 7x. Ensure that students understand how to write the reciprocal of an algebraic fraction for use in division.

In this small step, students explore multiplicative relationships between quantities that are in direct proportion. Double number lines can be useful representations to highlight relationships between quantities in proportion. Encourage the use of different methods to give students strategies for the variety of problems that can arise with direct proportion. For example, the unitary method can be used to work out the value of a single unit, whereas the scaling method uses multipliers rather than finding the unit cost. Encourage students to consider which is the most efficient method to use depending on the given information.

Use conversion graphs to convert between units. Provide students with conversion graphs and encourage them to draw vertical and horizontal lines for accurate conversions. Then give them opportunities to draw their own conversion graphs using relevant information. Students also work out conversions outside the range of a graph, using their understanding of direct proportion from the previous step. For example, if a graph shows 5 miles ≈ 8 km, then 50 miles ≈ 80 km. Include conversion graphs that are not in direct proportion, for example converting temperatures between Celsius and Fahrenheit.

In this small step, students build on the previous steps to convert between currencies. Begin with simple exchange rates involving integers, for example £1 = NZ$2 (New Zealand dollars), before using more realistic exchange rates. Encourage students to estimate their answers prior to calculating, to ensure that they have a sensible answer. Double number lines can be useful representations to help students explore a range of strategies to convert between different currencies. The use of calculators is recommended throughout this step.

In this small step, students explore graphical representations of direct proportion relationships, including revisiting conversion graphs. Highlight that direct proportion graphs form a straight line from the origin. Discuss everyday examples, for example the number of items sold and the cost, to help reinforce the main features of the graphs. Remind students of the importance of labelling the axes and using an appropriate scale. Ensure that students can draw a direct proportion graph from given information, as well as read from a direct proportion graph to complete a conversion. Encourage them to think about values outside the range of the graph.

In this small step, students explore relationships between similar shapes and calculate unknown lengths. Highlight that the corresponding lengths of similar shapes are in the same ratio. Focus on strategies to work out the scale factor of enlargement between two similar shapes, dividing one length by a corresponding length on the other shape, and using scale factors to work out unknown lengths. Show students similar shapes presented in different orientations. Exploration of examples and non-examples is useful to highlight the concept of similar shapes.

This small step reviews and extends Year 7 content, and students explore more complex conversions of length, mass and capacity. Rulers, measuring jugs and scales are useful in supporting students to understand the relative size of different measures. This also helps them to decide whether to multiply or divide a measure by a power of 10 to convert it, rather than relying on memory. Discussions about the prefixes “milli-”, “centi-” and “kilo-” may help students to understand relationships between different measures. Where appropriate, encourage students to work out conversions with more unfamiliar units, such as micrometres.

Draw and interpret scale diagrams. Encourage them to explore this step practically by creating and using scale diagrams. The link between scale, scale factors and ratio should be made explicit. This could be reinforced by linking back to earlier representations, such as the double number line, to highlight links between actual lengths and lengths represented on a scale diagram. Examples of diagrams that are not to scale could also be useful to emphasise the key features of scale. Ensure the use of language such as “1 cm represents 50 m” instead of “1 cm equals 50 m”, as 1 cm 50 m.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Proportion and scale_8_Interpret maps using scale and ratios
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on the previous step to interpret distances on a map. Students should be confident with metric conversions of length before attempting this step. Highlight the multiplicative relationships between different values in a given scale. For example, if 1 cm represents 15 cm on a plan, then 2 cm represents 30 cm. Double number lines may be useful to support this idea. Provide students with opportunities to measure distances on a map, converting these to the actual distance using a given scale. Students should also be able to convert actual distances to their respective lengths on a map. Explore working with scales given as ratios, understanding that the values in the ratio represent the same units, for example 1 : 10 000 means that 1 cm represents 10 000 cm.

In this small step, students explore how ratio is used to represent multiplicative relationships between two or more values, and they are introduced to the colon in the context of a ratio. Highlight that a ratio is a comparison of two or more parts of a whole. Begin by using sentences, for example “For every 2 squares, there are 3 circles”, before writing this as a formal ratio. Emphasise the importance of the order of the terms within ratio notation. For example, if the ratio of red counters to yellow counters is 3 : 4, the ratio of yellow counters to red counters is 4 : 3. Bar models are a useful representation to emphasise the equal parts of a ratio. As their confidence develops, students can work with ratios that compare three or more quantities, for example 3 : 4 : 1

Find the ratio of a part to the whole when we know the whole. Divide an amount into a given ratio. Bar models are useful to represent what is known/unknown and to support students in understanding the calculations required. A comparison bar model is more useful than a single bar model, particularly for later steps where a difference is given. Ensure that students understand the terms “part” and “whole” and establish that they need to work out the total number of parts before dividing. Discuss adding the separate amounts at the end to check that they are equal to the original total. Provide students with opportunities to explore a range of problems, as well as ratios that compare three or more quantities.

In this small step, students solve problems involving a difference between two or more quantities of a ratio. Again, comparison bar models are useful representations. Encourage students to pay careful attention to where given information should be labelled on the bar models. Discuss the importance of drawing relatively accurate bar models, as those that are not proportional can lead to incorrect calculations. Drawing attention to similarities and differences between problems where a part, whole or difference is given will be useful to develop students’ understanding. Further opportunities to consolidate the many types of “sharing in a ratio” problems are provided later in the block.

Simplify ratios to their smallest integer terms. Students may be familiar with the concept of simplifying by finding common factors from simplifying fractions in Year 7. Ensure that they understand that a ratio can be simplified if all the values in a ratio share a common factor. Encourage them to identify the highest common factor, although comparing other strategies is also useful to encourage flexible thinking. Concrete resources such as cubes and counters can be used to support understanding. It may also be useful to look at the answers to questions in previous steps and simplify these to see how the original ratio is obtained.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Ratio (1)_6_Express ratios in the form 1:n and n:1 E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students extend the simplification techniques from the previous step to express a unit ratio. Students need to understand that when a ratio is written in the form 1 : n, the first quantity of the ratio has a value of 1 and the second quantity of the ratio (n) can be any value, including non-integer values, and vice versa for ratios written in the form n : 1. Discuss how it can be easier to compare ratios in this format, especially when dealing with proportional change.

In this small step, students explore how the parts in a ratio compare to each value in the ratio as a fraction of the whole. Using representations such as cubes and counters can be useful to highlight that a ratio compares one part of the whole to another part, whereas a fraction compares a part to the whole. Single bar models are easier than comparison bar models for comparing fractions and ratios. Encourage students to focus on how many parts there are in total before thinking about fractions. Provide them with opportunities to write both ratios as fractions and fractions as ratios. This step provides an opportunity to reinforce previous learning on making 1 whole from a given fraction or fractions.

Solve ratio problems in context, giving them the opportunity to consolidate and reinforce their understanding of ratio covered in the previous steps. Pay particular attention to problems involving sharing in a ratio. If using bar models, ensure that students label given information correctly to avoid potential errors. Comparing bar models for similar problems can be useful to remind students of the different strategies needed when sharing in a ratio. Also give students questions involving simplifying ratios, writing ratios in the forms 1 : n and n : 1, as well as working fluently with ratios and fractions. This step can be used to focus in on any areas of particular difficulty or to explore ratios in other topics such as geometry or algebra.

In this small step, students develop understanding of lines of symmetry, building on learning from Key Stage 2 Folding shapes made of paper can provide useful support, as can mirrors, particularly for checking answers. Once students are confident finding a single line in a shape (horizontal, vertical or diagonal), they can progress to identifying shapes that have more than one line of symmetry. They can also explore the structure of shapes and how this affects the number of lines of symmetry. Give students the opportunity to apply their learning to everyday objects, and discuss theoretical and actual symmetry and its imperfections.

In this small step, students are introduced to the concept of rotational symmetry and determine the order of rotational symmetry of a shape. It is important that students understand that all shapes have an order of rotational symmetry of at least 1, since any shape exists in its given orientation at least once during a full 360° rotation. Tracing paper can be helpful in identifying the order of rotational symmetry, but it is important to emphasise that the exact centre of the shape should be used. It can be useful for students to compare line and rotational symmetry of shapes to identify the differences and to understand that the number of lines of symmetry in a shape is not always equal to its order of rotational symmetry.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Autumn__Symmetry and reflection_6_Describe a reflection E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students use their understanding of reflection and symmetry to fully describe the single transformation from an object to an image after a reflection. Start with reflections of simple shapes such as rectangles and triangles. Discuss that the object and image are congruent and that each vertex from the object and image should be the same distance from the mirror line. Model finding the mirror line by counting the distance between the object and image and halving it. Using tracing paper or paper folding are also useful strategies. Once students are confident in identifying the position of the mirror line, discuss writing its equation. It may be helpful to recap the naming conventions of diagonal lines and equations of lines parallel to the axes.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Area volume and density_1_Name 2-D and 3-D shapes
candidate_ss_wr_desc: Naming 2-D and 3-D shapes with up to 12 sides. Focus on their key properties. Introduce the meaning of “-gon” as “angled” and explain how prefixes indicate the number of angles. For example, “hex-” means six, so a hexagon has six angles and, therefore, six sides. Direct students’ attention to key notations, such as those for right angles, equal angles, equal sides and parallel lines, emphasising the essential properties of each shape. Providing physical models of 3-D shapes can help students to confidently describe their properties. Recognising prisms is covered later in this block and properties of circles will be explored later in Year 8

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Area volume and density_2_Area of a 2-D shape
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students revisit Year 7 learning and calculate the areas of rectangles, parallelograms, triangles and trapezia. Encourage students to explore the links between the areas of different shapes. For example, a parallelogram can be transformed into a rectangle by rearranging its sections or can be cut in half to show the area of a triangle. Using dynamic geometry software can help to visually demonstrate these relationships. Students may need help to identify the perpendicular height of shapes. Model working with shapes in different orientations and shapes with more than two dimensions labelled. Students can use calculators to enable them to focus on choosing and using the correct formulae. If appropriate, challenge students to find the areas of shapes that require unit conversions.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Area volume and density_3_Area of a compound shape
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the areas of compound shapes. Start by splitting a compound shape into two smaller shapes and working out the area of each, then using these to work out the total area of the compound shape. Introduce examples that include all dimensions and those that require splitting into more than two shapes. Students may need support with identifying unknown lengths in compound shapes. Provide a range of examples that require dimensions to be added as well as subtracted.

In this small step, students deepen their understanding of 3-D shapes and identify the defining features of prisms. Model and encourage the use of key mathematical language, emphasising the differences between the vocabulary used to describe 3-D and 2-D shapes, such as comparing “edges” with “sides”. Establish that prisms have a constant cross-sectional area along their length. 3-D models or dynamic software can help to illustrate the properties of a prism. Show prisms in different orientations to prevent misconceptions, noting that the length of the prism can sometimes be referred to as its height. Explore non-examples such as pyramids, cones, cylinders and spheres, to help distinguish prisms from other shapes.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Area volume and density_5_Volume of cubes and cuboids
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the volumes of cubes and cuboids. Clarify that volume measures the space inside a 3-D object and is expressed in cubic units, while area measures the space in two dimensions. Use physical models such as interlocking cubes to help students visualise how volume fills a 3-D shape. Begin by counting layers of cubes before introducing the formula volume = length × width × height. Discuss how the three dimensions can be used interchangeably, and that the word “depth” may also be used. Model looking at cuboids from different orientations to identify the dimensions. Remind students that cubes are special cuboids, in which the dimensions are all equal, so the formula simplifies to the cube of the side length. If appropriate, challenge students to calculate the volumes of cuboids that require unit conversions.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Area volume and density_6_Convert metric units of mass and capacity
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students understand and use metric units of mass and capacity. Define the key units and their relationships. For example, 1000 mg is equivalent to 1 g, 1000 g is equivalent to 1 kg and 1000 kg is equivalent to 1 tonne. For capacity, focus on millilitres (ml), centilitres (cl) and litres (l), highlighting that 1000 ml is equivalent to 100 cl and 1 l. Emphasise that metric prefixes remain consistent, with “milli-” meaning one-thousandth and “kilo-” meaning one thousand, reinforcing conversions based on powers of 10 If appropriate, introduce 1 cm3 being equal to 1 ml, explaining how capacity is a measurable volume. Alongside conversion calculations, encourage discussion on selecting appropriate units for different items.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Area volume and density_7_Understand the units of density, mass and volume
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore density, mass and volume, developing a deeper understanding of the units involved. Introduce density through familiar comparisons, such as looking at how the same mass of different materials occupies different amounts of space. For example, ask if a tonne of bricks takes up the same volume as a tonne of feathers. For objects of similar size, discuss why their masses differ, reinforcing the link between mass, volume and density. Emphasise the importance of using the correct units and introduce the concept of “per” (mass per unit volume) by relating it to familiar concepts such as mph or km/h. Examine the density of various materials, including solids, liquids and gases, across different volumes and encourage discussion on selecting appropriate units for different objects.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Area volume and density_8_Solve problems with density, mass and volume
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on the previous step to solve problems with density, mass and volume. Reinforce that density is the mass per unit of volume and introduce the formula, density = mass volume . It can be helpful to model the calculation of density using a range of common materials, for example wood, metal and plastic, asking students to consider if they think the material will be more or less dense than the previous one. Once students are confident with calculating the density of an object, they can use the formula to calculate the volume or mass of an object. Calculators can be used for support. Encourage students to check that their answers and units make sense for the given context.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Equations and inequalities_10_Solve inequalities with unknowns on both sides E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students develop their understanding of solving equations with unknowns on both sides to solving inequalities. Before introducing inequalities, recap strategies to solve equations with unknowns on both sides, highlighting which unknown has the smaller coefficient. Ensure that students pay attention to inequality symbols used and encourage discussions about integer values that satisfy each inequality. Practice should include examples of inequalities with brackets or of different forms, for example 3 + x < 5x − 1 If appropriate, students could also build on their understanding from the previous step, forming and solving inequalities with unknowns on both sides.

In this small step, students develop understanding of solving 1- and 2-step equations, building on learning from Year 7 This step provides opportunities to consolidate understanding of arithmetic with directed number, solving equations such as c + 5 = −2 and 3p + 17 = 11, introduced earlier in Year 8, where students used directed number with algebra. They also solve equations in different forms, for example 10 = 5k and 19 = 2x + 1, and practise writing non-integer solutions as both decimals and fractions. Throughout the step, refer to letters as “unknowns” rather than “variables”, as there is only one possible solution for these types of equations.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Equations and inequalities_2_Solve more complex equations
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students solve equations with brackets and negative coefficients of an unknown. Start with strategies to solve equations involving brackets, ensuring that students are confident expanding single brackets. Discuss other strategies, for example dividing by the coefficient of a bracket as a first step. Students can then explore equations with negative coefficients of an unknown, for example 10 − 2x = 4. Encourage them to add 2x to both sides of the equation as a first step. Discuss other strategies, for example dividing both sides by the negative coefficient of the unknown. Questions should include non-integer and negative solutions.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Equations and inequalities_4_Form and solve equations
candidate_ss_wr_desc: Forming expressions and solving equations. Ensure that students are confident forming expressions, covered earlier in Year 8. Where appropriate, recap topics to allow a variety of contexts in which to form equations, for example area and perimeter of shapes or angle facts. Start with forming and solving 1-step equations, before moving on to more complex equations such as those covered in Steps 2 and 3. Model how to form an equation from given information, for example equating an expression to a known value. Forming equations with unknowns on both sides is covered in the next step.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Equations and inequalities_5_Solve equations with unknowns on both sides
candidate_ss_wr_desc: Solving 2-step equations with unknowns on both sides. Bar models are useful to introduce the strategies required to solve these equations. Encourage students to identify which of the two coefficients of the unknown is smaller. Discuss why subtracting this from both sides is a useful first step, highlighting that this reduces the equation to a 1- or 2-step equation. Ensure that students are comfortable representing solutions in multiple forms, for example x = 3 or 3 = x. Once students are confident, include questions with non-integer and negative solutions. If appropriate, students could also explore equations in which adding an unknown to both sides is an efficient first step, for example 10 − x = 2x + 1

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Equations and inequalities_6_Understand and use inequalities
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students learn how to interpret and use inequalities. Students may be familiar with inequality symbols from Key Stage 2 when comparing values, for example 5 < 9 Establish that an inequality describes a range of values. Highlight the difference between similar inequalities, for example x < 5 and x ≤ 5, explaining that the range of values for the second inequality includes the value of 5. Encourage students to discuss possible values that satisfy an inequality. Students should also explore compound inequalities, for example 3 < n < 7, again discussing possible values that satisfy the inequality.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Equations and inequalities_7_Inequalities on a number line
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on the previous step to represent inequalities on a number line. Students learn that inequalities using the symbols < or > are represented by an unshaded circle above the number given, and inequalities using the symbols ≤ or ≥ by a shaded circle above the number. Providing students with varied practice can be an effective way to highlight the differences between representations on a number line, for example representing x > 5 and x ≥ 5 Students also represent and interpret compound inequalities on number lines, understanding that this is represented with two circles joined by a straight line segment.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Indices_1_Add and subtract expressions with indices
candidate_ss_wr_desc: Add and subtract expressions with indices, simplifying by collecting like terms with the same varaible and exponent. Begin with variables with powers up to 3, as students are already familiar with squares and cubes. As confidence develops, introduce higher powers. It may be helpful to recap the meaning of “like” and “unlike” terms. Students may also need a reminder about the meaning of “coefficient” and the convention of omitting 1 as a coefficient. Encourage students to use the identity symbol. Using manipulatives, such as algebra tiles, can effectively illustrate why, for example, 2x² + 3x² æ 5x², not 5x4

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Indices_2_Multiply and divide expressions with indices
candidate_ss_wr_desc: Multiply and divide expressions with indices, by simplifying expressions. Remind students of the conventions for expressions such as 3 × a, b × 4 and c × c, as well as the use of fractions to represent division. Students explore powers, for example recognising that x5 is equivalent to x × x × x × x × x. Encourage them to write calculations out in full to help develop understanding, for example 3 cubed divided by 3 squared = 3 × 3 × 3 divided by 3 × 3 . This will help to prepare them for higher powers and the laws of indices later in the block. Also remind students to express answers in fractional form, such as y divided by 2 , rather than using decimals (0.5y).

Subtraction law of indices. Encourage students to write out the multiplications indicated by the index notation, for example 3 to the power 5 divided by 3 to the power 3 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 divided by 3 × 3 × 3 , and then to identify terms that can be cancelled out. Reinforce that terms are cancelled because 3 divied by 3 = 1. Encourage students to generalise the rule for dividing terms with the same base, leading to am ÷ an = am − n. Remind them that, as for the addition law of indices, this rule only applies when the bases are the same. Throughout this step, students work with both numerical and algebraic expressions.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Indices_5_Addition and subtraction laws for indices
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate their understanding from the previous two steps by applying both the addition and subtraction laws of indices. If necessary, remind students of the general rules am × an = am + n and am ÷ an = am − n. They should identify which rule to apply and work with expressions that include a combination of multiplication and division. Emphasise that these laws only apply when the bases are the same. Students also explore powers of zero, reasoning why t2 t2 is equal to t0 and 1. Challenge them to extend their thinking with questions involving multiple bases and operations, for example a5 × b3 ÷ a2 × b6

In this extend step, students explore powers of powers, building on their prior knowledge of the laws of indices. Start with examples such as (54)3, showing that it can be rewritten as 54 × 54 × 54. Using their understanding of the addition law of indices, students should then deduce that (54)3 = 512, leading to the general rule (ax)y æ axy. Students practise applying this rule with both numerical and algebraic bases. Once confident, they could extend their understanding to expressions involving coefficients, for example (2x4)5. Remind students of the order of operations to ensure accurate calculations.

In this extend step, students explore negative indices, building on their knowledge of reciprocals and negative powers of 10, which may have been covered as an extend step in Year 7 A useful way to develop this concept is by identifying a pattern when decreasing the power, for example 102 = 100, 101 = 10, 100 = 1, 10−1 = 1 10 . This illustrates that each time the power decreases, the value is divided by the base, which can be expressed as a fraction. Once students are confident in their understanding of a power of −1, they move on to exploring powers of −2 and lower. Emphasise that the power still applies to the numerator and denominator once the number is expressed as a fraction, for example 5−2 = 12 52 = 1 25. This helps to reinforce the pattern that negative exponents represent the reciprocal of the base raised to the corresponding positive power.

In this extend step, students explore fractional indices. Start with unit fractional indices with numerical bases. Explain that the denominator of a fractional exponent indicates the root, for example 9 1 2 = 9 and 27 1 3 = 27 3 Once students are confident in evaluating fractional indices, they explore non-integer bases, focusing on fractions and decimals that comprise square or cube numbers, for example 25 64 and 0.81. Students do not need to work with non-unit fractional indices in this block, as these are covered in Year 10

In this small step, students build on their understanding of expressing one value as a percentage of another, now focusing on percentage change. Ensure that students are confident finding the difference and identifying the original amount before writing the fraction in the form difference original . Remind them that if the denominator is a factor or multiple of 100, they can scale the fraction accordingly, whereas for other cases they can use the general formula difference original × 100. It is also beneficial to examine problems that can be solved using both calculator and non-calculator methods, encouraging students to choose the most efficient approach.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Percentages_11_Find the original value given a percentage
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students determine the original amount from a given percentage. This may have been introduced as an extend step in Year 7, but this step also includes percentages greater than 100%. Emphasise that the original value represents 100%. Start with percentages that are easy to scale, for example 50%, 20% and 10%. Bar models are a useful representation to help students understand the percentage that the amount represents. Students could then explore other percentages such as 80%, 15% and 125%. They could use a scaling method or inverse operations with multipliers to find the original amount. For example, if 80% of £200 is calculated by 200 × 0.8 = 160, then 160 ÷ 0.8 = 200

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Percentages_12_Choose appropriate methods to solve percentage problems
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate their learning about percentages by applying their knowledge to solve problems. There should be an emphasis on choice of strategy rather than arithmetic, so the use of calculators is encouraged, if appropriate. Model reading questions, asking students what they know and what they need to find out, while highlighting key words. Students can continue to use bar models to represent the problems, allowing them to identify what information is given and what needs to be worked out. Prompt students to check whether their answer is reasonable by considering it in the context of the question.

In this small step, students review their understanding of calculating percentages of amounts from Year 7, using calculator and non-calculator methods. Knowledge of multipliers is not required at this stage, as it will be introduced later in the block. Recap methods for finding common percentages such as 1%, 5%, 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% (the whole amount) without a calculator. Using bar models can support students’ understanding, where appropriate. Once they are confident, introduce more complex percentages, for example 17%. Discuss how to combine common percentages to form 17%, for example 10% + 5% + 1% + 1%. Comparing this approach to a calculator method can help to reinforce the idea that once students determine 1%, they can find any percentage.

In this small step, students convert between decimals and percentages, building on their Year 7 understanding of fractions, decimals and percentages. This step will build the foundational knowledge required for calculating with multipliers later in the block. Remind students that a percentage means “number of parts per 100” and emphasise the connection to place value and fractions, for example 0.34 = 34 hundredths = 34% = 34 100 . Students convert decimals to percentages and vice versa, focusing on percentages less than 100%. A hundred square can be a useful visual aid to reinforce understanding.

In this small step, students build on their understanding of calculating percentages and converting between decimals and percentages from previous steps. They now use multipliers to find a percentage of an amount, focusing on percentages less than 100%, as percentages greater than 100% will be covered in later steps. Percentage increases using multipliers will be introduced later in the block. Start by reinforcing the relationship between decimals and percentages, for example recognising that 34% is equivalent to 0.34. Discuss how the wording of questions can guide the necessary calculations. For example, when finding 34% of 500, the word “of” in mathematics often signifies multiplication, so the calculation can be written as 34% × 500 or 500 × 0.34

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Percentages_4_Convert between percentages and decimals greater than 1
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on their prior knowledge of converting between percentages and decimals, now focusing on values greater than 1. This step prepares students to calculate percentage increases using a multiplier. Reinforce the understanding that a percentage means “number of parts per 100”. If necessary, connect this concept to partitioning, for example 130% = 100% + 30%, and relate this to its decimal equivalent of 1.3 = 1 + 0.3. Encourage students to explore whether percentages greater than 100% make sense in different contexts, for example receiving 25% extra time in an exam means being given 125% of the standard time. Compare situations where such percentages are possible and where they are not.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Percentages_7_Percentage increase and decrease using a multiplier
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate their learning from the previous steps and calculate percentage increase and decrease using multipliers. They practise a mixture of questions to ensure that they are thinking carefully and not just following a procedure. Discuss the multipliers for increasing or decreasing by, for example, 60%, 6% and 0.6%. Drawing bar models to identify whether the problem represents a percentage increase or decrease and to determine the correct multiplier can be useful. Discuss the key vocabulary to help students recognise increases and decreases, such as a car depreciating in value.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Percentages_8_Express one number as a fraction or a percentage of another no calculator
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students express one number as a fraction or percentage of another. Start by writing one number as a fraction of another, ensuring that students are confident with this before moving on to percentages. Initially, focus on fractions where the denominator is a factor or multiple of 100, encouraging students to use their knowledge of equivalent fractions to scale the denominator to 100 by multiplying or dividing before converting to a percentage. They should also work with fractions that, when simplified, have a denominator that is a factor of 100. Where appropriate, students could express values such as 1 out of 8 as a percentage, building on their prior knowledge of converting eighths to percentages from Year 7

In this small step, students differentiate between discrete, continuous, quantitative and qualitative data. Explain that discrete data consists of countable values (for example, the number of tickets sold at a cinema), while continuous data can take any value within a given range and can include decimals and fractions (for example, temperature). Establish that quantitative data is numerical (for example, the number of goals scored in a football match), whereas qualitative data is non-numerical (for example, eye colour). It is important for students to understand how the type of data affects the choice of graphs or averages used in analysis. Encourage them to discuss why qualitative and discrete data are often represented using bar charts, pie charts or pictograms, while line graphs and scatter graphs are typically used to represent continuous data.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Types of data_3_Choose the most appropriate average
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students identify and understand outliers and errors in data sets. Discuss that outliers are numbers that are very different from the rest of the data. Highlight that outliers could be real, unusual values or errors in the data collection. Show examples of data from everyday life and ask students to consider reasons for the outliers. They could also link this step to outliers they have seen in scatter diagrams, improving their ability to notice data that does not follow a pattern. Emphasise the effects that outliers have on averages and range, and discuss the effect of calculating these without including an outlier.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Types of data_4_Compare distributions using averages and the range
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students continue to develop their understanding of averages, considering when an average (mean, median or mode) for a given data set is appropriate. Discuss the characteristics and limitations of each type of average and when each one is the most suitable representation of “typical” in a set of data. This approach draws students’ attention to a complete data set rather than just performing calculations. Everyday applications, such as wages, demonstrate that the median or mode can provide a more representative summary than the mean, particularly when outliers are present.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Types of data_5_Averages from an ungrouped frequency table
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students continue developing their understanding of averages and range by comparing data sets using these measures. Draw students’ attention to the range as a measure of spread, helping them to understand that it indicates how consistent the data is. When comparing data sets, considering both the average and the range together provides a fuller picture of the data set’s typical values and variability. Examples in context, such as comparing sports teams’ performance statistics, can help students to see how different averages together with the range offer insights into consistency and variation across data sets.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Types of data_6_Represent and interpret grouped discrete data
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the mean, median and mode from ungrouped frequency tables. When calculating the mean, begin by organising raw data into a table, listing data values together with how often they occur. Model how to find the total of each sub-category, before adding all the products together and dividing by the total number of data values. To find the modal value, encourage students to consider the values within a category that occur most often. Support students finding the median from a table by initially writing the data from the frequency table in a list. Highlight the connection between the median from the list and its location in the table, before modelling how to find the median directly from the table using the cumulative frequency.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Types of data_7_Represent and interpret continuous data grouped into
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students represent and interpret grouped discrete data in frequency tables, without inequalities. The use of inequality notation will be covered in the next step. Discuss when it is appropriate to use grouped data, focusing on simplifying large data sets. Explain that each data point should fall into one distinct group, so the groups should be structured in a way that avoids any ambiguity, such as using the intervals 0–10, 11–20 and so on. It can be helpful to discuss sensible group intervals. For example, for a data set with a range of 100, two intervals of 0–50 and 51–100 may be less appropriate than smaller intervals such as 0–20 and so on. Students calculate the frequency for each interval and the cumulative frequency of multiple intervals.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Spring__Types of data_8_Mean and mode from a grouped frequency table E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students represent and interpret continuous data using grouped frequency tables with equal class intervals. Recap interpreting inequalities, for example 5 < x ≤ 10, and emphasise that continuous data encompasses a range of values within a given interval. Highlight why < and ≤ symbols are necessary to avoid overlaps between intervals and discuss which interval borderline values should be put into. A number line can be useful to illustrate how boundaries separate each interval. Also discuss how to interpret the grouped data, for example identifying intervals with the greatest frequencies. Address the limitations of grouped data, such as the loss of individual data values.

small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Angles in parallel lines and polygons_10_Interior angles of a regular polygon
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students build on learning from the previous steps to find the sizes of unknown angles in regular polygons. Start by discussing the term “regular”, as students often misunderstand this to mean only equal lengths, rather than equal lengths and equal angles. Compare different methods to work out the size of one interior angle. Once students are confident in working out unknown angles in a single polygon, move on to examples of compound shapes made from regular polygons. Encourage students to give reasons for each stage of their workings. This step provides an opportunity for students to determine and apply the most suitable method for each question. Calculators may be used throughout this step, so that the focus remains on the method rather than the arithmetic. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse interior and exterior angles. • Students may confuse the size of interior angles with the interior angle sum. • Students may believe that all interior angles are equal in size, even when the polygon is irregular. small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Angles in parallel lines and polygons_11_Prove simple geometric facts  E
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students begin to prove or disprove simple geometric facts. Start with formal proofs of facts that students are already familiar with, such as proving that the sum of angles in a triangle is 180°. Highlight the difference between a proof and a demonstration by comparing a formal method with a visual approach such as tearing the corners off a triangle to show that they form a straight line. Once confident, students can move on to simple “show that” activities and begin to become familiar with the language when testing conjectures. Emphasise the importance of labelling diagrams, justifying each stage of their workings and using correct angle notation. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may mistakenly think that a visual demonstration is a formal proof. • Students may believe that providing examples is enough to prove a general statement. • Students may not use correct angle and line notation. • Students may not label their diagrams correctly. small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Angles in parallel lines and polygons_1_Basic angle rules and notation
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students review the basic rules of angles and notation covered in Year 7 Start by looking at each rule in isolation: the sum of angles on a straight line, angles around a point and angles in triangles and quadrilaterals. Students should be able to identify when angles sum to 180° or 360° and when angles are equal. Once they are confident in identifying the correct rule, move on to diagrams where more than one rule may need to be applied. Remind students of the three-letter angle notation, which is used throughout the block. Encourage them to explain and justify how they identify and calculate angles, using correct vocabulary and angle rules. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the different rules relating to angles in lines and shapes. • Students may confuse instances when angles sum to 180° and when they sum to 360°. • Students may believe that angles on the same straight line that do not meet still sum to 180°. • In their calculations, students may not account for angles that are not labelled. small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Angles in parallel lines and polygons_5_Solve problems with angles in parallel lines
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use the angle facts covered in the previous steps to solve more complex, multi-step problems. Model the thought processes involved when approaching problem-solving questions. Verbalise each step to help students understand how to break down a problem, identify key information and decide which mathematical strategy to apply. Throughout this step, encourage students to label their diagrams, show their workings clearly and justify their answers using correct angle notation and vocabulary. Ensure that students check their answers throughout. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misapply the rules for alternate and corresponding angles. • Students may mistakenly believe that pairs of angles are equal in situations where they sum to 180°, or vice versa. • Students may not recognise pairs of alternate, corresponding or co-interior angles in more complex diagrams or problems. small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Angles in parallel lines and polygons_7_Find unknown lengths and angles in special quadrilaterals
candidate_ss_wr_desc: Work out unknown sides and angles of special quadrilaterals. Throughout this step, students apply their knowledge of angle facts, particularly that angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360° and the properties of angles in parallel lines, to make deductions and justify their answers. Start with quadrilaterals in isolation before moving on to compound shapes and more complex diagrams involving quadrilaterals. Encourage students to discuss and label the information on the diagrams and to use correct angle notation and vocabulary to give reasons for their answers. Calculators can be used to ensure that the focus is on angle reasoning rather than arithmetic. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that all quadrilaterals have equal sides and equal angles. • Students may confuse the properties of specific quadrilaterals. • Students may misapply angle facts and properties of shapes. • Students may not give sufficient reasons for their answers. small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Angles in parallel lines and polygons_8_Exterior angles of a polygon
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the exterior angles of a polygon. Discuss the definition of a polygon, using examples and non-examples to support understanding. Ensure that students are familiar with exterior angles, understanding that they are formed by extending the sides of a polygon and not that they are the remaining angle around the point at each vertex. Establish the relationship between interior and exterior angles, recognising that the two angles will form a straight line and therefore sum to 180°. Then move on to deduce that the exterior angle sum of any polygon is 360°. Ensure that students understand that the exterior angles will only ever be equal when the polygon is regular. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that the exterior angle is the remaining angle around a point, rather than being formed by extending the sides of the polygon. • Students may believe that the exterior angle sum varies, depending on the number of sides of the polygon. • Students may believe that the sum of interior and exterior angles is 360° rather than 180°. small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Angles in parallel lines and polygons_9_Interior angles of a polygon
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students explore the interior angles of a polygon. Ensure that students are aware that the sum of the interior angle and the exterior angle at a vertex is 180°. Once students are secure in this, move on to calculating the interior angle sum. Use diagrams to explore the relationship between the number of sides a polygon has and the number of internal triangles that can be formed within it. This will lead students to deduce that the interior angle sum is equal to (n − 2 ) × 180°, where n is the number of sides. Challenge students to work out the sizes of unknown angles in a polygon by calculating the interior angle sum. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that the interior angle sum is the same for all polygons. • Students may believe that the interior angle sum is found by multiplying the number of sides by 180 • Students may believe that all polygons have equal interior angles. In this small step, students are introduced to pi (π) and explore the relationship between a circle’s diameter and its circumference. Students should discover that the circumference is always a little more than three times the diameter, so the ratio of circumference to diameter is constant. This consistent ratio leads to the formula π = circumference diameter . Students can then make links to the formulae C = πd and C = 2πr. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may select the wrong total, for example using the whole group when the question refers to a subset. • Students may confuse which branch of the tree to use for a given event. • Students may identify the correct frequency and state this instead of giving the answer as a probability. In this small step, students are introduced to key vocabulary that underpins future probability work. Students explore the meaning of terms such as “event”, “outcome”, “certain”, “impossible”, “even chance”, “likely” and “unlikely”. Take time to consider each term in context, using everyday examples to support understanding. Encourage students to identify what the event is and the possible outcomes, and to begin reflecting on factors that affect the likelihood of an event happening, such as forecasting the weather or making decisions based on previous outcomes. Bias can be explored by asking students to consider situations such as comparing a fair spinner to a weighted spinner, to show how unequal likelihood affects probability. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that all events have an equal chance of happening or not happening. • Students may believe that recent outcomes affect future results. • Students may think that an event and an outcome are the same. In this small step, students build on the previous step to place events on a probability scale from zero to 1 Students connect qualitative descriptions (impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain) with numerical values, recognising that probability can be represented as a number between zero and 1. This builds on their experience with number lines and provides an opportunity to apply knowledge of fractions, decimals and percentages in a new context. It also offers valuable revision of equivalence and ordering. Emphasise that probability is a measure of likelihood. Encourage students to use the vocabulary from the previous step to justify where they place events on the scale. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may assume that all probabilities are written as fractions. • Students may neglect the fact that all probabilities need to be between zero and 1. For example, a probability of 25% is possible but a probability of 25 is not. • Students may misplace probabilities on the scale because of errors made when converting between fractions and decimals. small_step_id: Year 8_12-13_Summer__Tables and probability_3_Probability of a single event ​
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students calculate the probability of a single event and are introduced to the notation P(event). Use concrete resources such as dice, coins, spinners and coloured counters in a bag to establish that probability is calculated as number of successful outcomes total number of equally likely outcomes . Emphasise that probabilities can be written as fractions, decimals or percentages, but not in ratio notation. Discuss the concept of bias, emphasising that this method is only valid when all outcomes are equally likely. This step also provides an opportunity to practise converting between fractions, decimals and percentages in the context of probability. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may assume that all outcomes are equally likely, even when they are not. • Students may describe the probability in words rather than calculating it as a fraction/decimal/percentage. • Students may use incorrect total outcomes when interpreting word problems.
