How can you show A B on a Venn diagram? • How do you read A B out loud? • What part of the diagram should be shaded? • How does the shading show “in A or in B or in both”? • Does the union include the elements that are in both sets? Explain how you know. • If A = { a, b, c } and B = { c, d, e }, what are the elements of A B? Explain your answer. • If ξ = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 }, A = { 1, 2, 3 } and B = { 2, 3, 4 }, what are the elements of A B? Explain your answer. • How is the union different from the intersection? • Can a union of two sets ever have fewer elements than either set on its own? Explain your answer. • Is the union of two sets always bigger than their intersection? Explain your answer. Union of sets Year 9 | Summer term | Block 3 – Sets and probability | Step 3

small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_4_Complement of a set (E)
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students explore the complement of a set and its representation using set notation. Remind students that the universal set, ξ, is the complete collection of objects or numbers under consideration. Explain that the complement of a set contains all the elements in the universal set that are not in a set. Use clear examples to model this idea; for example, if ξ is the set of integers from 1 to 10 inclusive and A = { 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 }, then the complement of A, written as A′, is { 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 }. Encourage students to write complements using set notation and to describe them in words, such as “the set of integers from 1 to 10 that are not even”. As students gain confidence, highlight how complements help them to see how sets and their opposites fit within the universal set. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to take the complement of a set without reference to the universal set, ξ, leading to inconsistent answers. • Students may think that complement means the “opposite”, rather than exclusion. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_5_Probability of a single event ​
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students consolidate and build on learning from Year 8, using probability notation such as P(heads), expressing probabilities as fractions, decimals and percentages, and using the property that probabilities sum to 1 Introduce mutually exclusive events through simple cases, such as rolling a 2 or a 6 on a dice, to illustrate how probabilities can be added. small_step_id: Year 9_13-14_Summer__Sets and probability_6_Use diagrams to work out probabilities
candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this small step, students use two-way tables, frequency trees and sample space diagrams to work out probabilities. Explore one diagram at a time. Model how outcomes in a two-way table are placed in rows and columns so that totals can be completed and used to find probabilities. In this small step, students explore relative frequency through experiments and recorded results. Emphasise how the relative frequency of an outcome fluctuates with a small number of trials, but as more trials are completed it stabilises. This shows the link between probability and relative frequency, with probability seen as the value that relative frequency approaches in the long run. Discuss how short-term variation becomes less significant as the number of trials increases, so results move closer to the theoretical probability, making larger samples more reliable. Graphs can make these patterns clearer, and computer simulations allow students to see behaviour. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that relative frequency and probability are the same. • Students may not recognise that conducting more trials increases the accuracy of the relative frequency. • Students may think that results should reflect theoretical probability after only a few trials, without recognising the effect of short-term variation. • Students may think that if an outcome has not occurred for a while, then it is certain to happen soon. National Curriculum links • Record, describe and analyse the frequency of outcomes of simple probability experiments involving randomness, fairness, equally and unequally likely outcomes, using appropriate language and the 0–1 probability scale Mathematical talk • How is relative frequency calculated? In this small step, students explore expected outcomes, building on their knowledge of relative frequency and experimental probability. Highlight that expected outcomes represent a long-term average, rather than a precise prediction for individual trials. Variability can be illustrated through experiments, showing that results may differ from the calculated expectation, particularly with smaller samples. For example, if the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair dice is 1 6, then in 60 rolls the expected outcome would be ten 6s, although the actual result may vary. Ensure that students practise calculating expected outcomes when probabilities are expressed as fractions, decimals or percentages, and compare these with experimental results. Using tables, graphs or simulations helps to make the patterns more visible and reinforces the link between expected outcomes and probability. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that the expected outcome is what will happen in practice, rather than an estimation. • Students may believe that variation from the expected outcome means that the calculation is incorrect. National Curriculum links • Record, describe and analyse the frequency of outcomes of simple probability experiments involving randomness, fairness, equally and unequally likely outcomes, using appropriate language and the 0–1 probability scale. Mathematical talk • What does “expected outcome” mean? • If the probability of an event is 1 4, how many times would you expect it to occur in 40 trials? How many times would you expect it to occur in 400/4000 trials? • Can the actual results be different from the expected results? In this small step, students explore independent events. It can be helpful to introduce the idea through a sample space diagram, for example for rolling two dice, where all possible outcomes can be listed and favourable cases counted. Draw students’ attention to how this method produces the same result as multiplying the separate probabilities, for example 1 2 × 1 6 = 1 12 for rolling an even number on one dice and a 5 on the other. Making this connection explains why multiplication is used for independent events and helps to link different approaches. Encourage students to express probabilities as both fractions and decimals, supporting fluency and making comparisons easier. Using diagrams provides opportunities for students to develop accurate reasoning. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think that “independent” means that the probabilities are equal, rather than that one outcome does not affect the other. • Students may confuse independent with mutually exclusive events, not recognising that mutually exclusive outcomes cannot happen together. In this small step, students build on their understanding from Year 8, completing and describing reflections in horizontal, vertical and diagonal lines. Some students may not yet have encountered reflections in lines expressed algebraically, or fully described reflections, as these are covered in extend steps in Year 8 Recap how to identify equations of vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines, as this underpins both drawing and describing reflections. Emphasise that a full description must include both the fact that it is a reflection and the equation of the mirror line. As with previous transformations, tracing paper is a useful tool. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not use the perpendicular distance between vertices and a diagonal mirror line. • Students may draw an incorrect reflection when a shape crosses one of the axes. • Students may incorrectly plot lines of the form y = a and x = b, resulting in an incorrect reflection. • Students may use non-mathematical vocabulary to describe a reflection, such as “flip” or “mirror”, rather than “reflect”. candidate_ss_wr_desc: In this extend step, students consolidate their understanding of reflections, translations, rotations and enlargements, applying a series of transformations to a shape. This step provides opportunities for students to discuss misconceptions or errors related to each of the four transformations. Highlight that changing the order of transformations can affect the final image. As with previous steps, model different transformations to students. Once confident, students could be encouraged to consider whether a series of transformations can sometimes be represented by a single transformation. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may carry out the transformations in an incorrect order. • Students may misinterpret key information, for example reflecting in the line y = 2 rather than x = 2 • Students may perform a second transformation on the original shape, rather than on the new image. National Curriculum links • Identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections applied to given figures • Identify and construct congruent triangles, and construct similar shapes by enlargement, with and without coordinate grids Mathematical talk • Does it matter which order the transformations are carried out? Explain how you know. • If you reflect a shape, then rotate the image, will the result be the same as rotating the shape first and then reflecting the image? Explain how you know. • What will the coordinates of the point ( , ) be if the shape is reflected in the x-axis, followed by a reflection in the y-axis? • Why do you perform the second transformation on the image, rather than the original shape? • Is there a single transformation that maps shape A onto shape C? • How can you check that the transformations have been drawn accurately? In this extend step, students enlarge shapes using a negative scale factor. Establish that enlarging by a negative scale factor changes both the size and orientation of a shape. Using ray lines to model this process is recommended, as the vertices of the object and image will lie on the same ray lines drawn from the centre of enlargement. Make links between positive and negative scale factors, for example comparing enlargements with scale factors of 2 and −2. If appropriate, students can also investigate negative fractional scale factors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may enlarge by a positive scale factor, rather than a negative scale factor. • Students may think that a negative scale factor produces a smaller shape. • Students may assume that negative and positive scale factors of the same magnitude, for example 2 and −2, produce identical results. National Curriculum links • Identify and construct congruent triangles, and construct similar shapes by enlargement, with and without coordinate grids Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about enlarging by a positive scale factor and enlarging by a negative scale factor? • Does an enlargement always have the same orientation as the original shape? Explain how you know. • Describe what happens when a shape is enlarged by a negative scale factor. • If a point is 4 units to the left of the centre of enlargement, where will its image be when enlarged by a scale factor of −2? • Why is it useful to draw ray lines when enlarging a shape? • In which quadrant will the image be after an enlargement of scale factor , about centre of enlargement ? • How can you check that an enlargement has been drawn accurately? In this small step, students describe enlargements using precise language. Explain that a full description of an enlargement must include both the scale factor of enlargement and the coordinates of the centre of enlargement. Remind students of strategies to calculate the scale factor of enlargement, such as dividing corresponding side lengths and ensuring that they divide the enlarged length by the original length. Model how to construct ray lines to locate the coordinates of the centre of enlargement. If necessary, use sentence stems to support students in structuring their response. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not describe an enlargement fully, for example only stating the scale factor. • Students may use additive rather than multiplicative reasoning to identify a scale factor. • Students may interpret enlargements incorrectly, for example stating a scale factor of 2 rather than 1 2 • Students may describe an enlargement in the wrong order, for example describing the enlargement of shape B to shape A, rather than shape A to shape B. National Curriculum links • Identify and construct congruent triangles, and construct similar shapes by enlargement, with and without coordinate grids Mathematical talk • What pieces of information do you need to describe an enlargement? • Why is it important to state the coordinates of the centre of enlargement? • Describe how you locate the coordinates of the centre of enlargement. • How can you use pairs of corresponding sides to calculate the scale factor? • How do you know when a shape has been enlarged by a fractional scale factor? • How does an enlargement by a scale factor of 2 differ from an enlargement by a scale factor of 1 2 ? • How could you check that your description of the enlargement is accurate? In this small step, students rotate a shape about a specific point. Model the process, clearly demonstrating how each vertex moves around the centre of rotation. Tracing paper is a useful tool for students, enabling them to mark both the object and the centre of rotation before physically rotating the shape. Encourage the use of a “north” arrow or similar reference line to support accurate turns of 90°, 180° and 270°. Highlight that rotations can be clockwise or anticlockwise and emphasise that the object and its image are always congruent, having the same size and shape, but in different orientations. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may rotate a shape about the origin rather than the stated centre of rotation. • Students may rotate a shape in the wrong direction. • Students may not rotate the correct number of degrees, for example rotating 180°, rather than 90°. • Students may not draw the image congruent to the original shape. Explain how you know. • Are any points invariant? Explain how you know. Rotation about a point Year 9 | Summer term | Block 4 – Transformations | Step 6

In this small step, students describe rotations using precise language. Emphasise that a full description must always include three key details: the angle of turn, the direction of turn (clockwise or anticlockwise) and the centre of rotation. Model the process clearly using tracing paper. A “north” arrow can also support students in identifying the direction and angle of turn. Encourage students to trial different centres of rotation, to establish a pair of suitable coordinates. If appropriate, use sentence stems to support students in structuring their answers. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not describe a rotation fully, for example not stating the direction. • Students may struggle to identify a centre of rotation, particularly if the centre is within a shape. • Students may not appreciate that, for example, a 90° rotation clockwise is equivalent to a 270° rotation anticlockwise. Use column vectors to carry out translations on a coordinate grid. Students should recognise that a translation produces a congruent shape with the same orientation. Model translating a shape, highlighting that the top number in a column vector represents horizontal movement and the bottom number represents vertical movement. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misinterpret a column vector, for example thinking that ( 2 3 ) means 2 up and 3 right. • Students may misinterpret negative values in column vectors, for example thinking that ( 1 −5) means 1 right and 5 up. • Students may only translate one vertex of the shape and incorrectly assume the positions of the remaining vertices. National Curriculum links • Identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections applied to given figures Mathematical talk • What does “translation” mean? • Does the size of the shape change after a translation? Explain how you know. • Why does a column vector contain two numbers? • What do the two numbers in a column vector tell you? • How can you describe the column vector in words? • What does the translation vector ( 2 −3) mean? • What happens if one of the numbers in the column vector is zero? • What is the difference between coordinates and a vector? • Why is it important to consider the scales of the axes when translating a shape? • How can you check that the translation has been completed accurately? Translation Year 9 | Summer term | Block 4 – Transformations | Step 8

In this small step, students describe a translation using a column vector. Encourage students to identify a pair of corresponding vertices, then model how to calculate the horizontal and vertical movements needed to map one onto the other. Reinforce that the order is important, with the horizontal movement being written as the top value in the vector and the vertical movement below. Emphasise that the same vector applies to every vertex of the shape, not just the pair chosen. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may use words instead of a column vector. • Students may incorrectly write the column vector as a coordinate or fraction. • Students may write the column vector incorrectly, for example ( 2 3 ) rather than ( 3 2 ) , or ( 5 2 ) instead of (−5 −2) . • Students may describe a translation in the wrong order, for example describing the transformation of shape B to shape A, rather than shape A to shape B. • Students may struggle to interpret translations with column vectors of the form ( 0 a ) or ( b 0 ) . National Curriculum links • Identify properties of, and describe the results of, translations, rotations and reflections applied to given figures Mathematical talk • How can you describe the translation in words?
